A release checklist starts with the change someone can actually see.
I draft the article before preparing the post and review the exact files before publishing.
What do you check before sharing a release?

blog.title: A practical checklist for sharing an app release
blog.description: A practical release writing checklist: gather public evidence, draft the article, review exact media and copy, and verify each published link.
blog.body:
A small release checklist makes it easier to explain what changed in an app and why the change matters. I start with the behavior a person can see, gather evidence from the public release, and write the explanation before preparing a social post. This example describes that process without claiming that a particular feature has shipped.

## Start with a visible change

The first question is what someone can do after the release that they could not do before it. A useful answer names an action and its result. It avoids implementation details unless those details help a developer understand a tradeoff. A screenshot can support the explanation, but it should show the actual result rather than a decorative screen.

I keep a short evidence list while drafting. Each claim points to a public release note, a public repository change, or an existing portfolio entry. If the evidence is missing, I remove the claim or leave the draft unfinished. This keeps a small update from turning into a promise about work that is still in progress.

The opening line should describe a real situation. For a developer tool, that might be a repeated manual step or a confusing error. For an app, it might be the task a person wants to finish. The rest of the explanation can then show the change in that context. A concrete opening also gives the reader a reason to keep reading.

## Prepare the article before the post

The article is the place for the full explanation. I write a short description, group the details under clear headings, and include enough context for someone who has never seen the project. The social copy comes from that article, with its own wording for each audience. A Russian channel post and an English developer discussion can describe the same release without being literal translations.

Before preparing media, I check the length of each caption. A short discussion post should leave room for a useful question. An image caption needs an accurate description of the picture. Any text placed on a cover has to survive the platform crop and remain clear on a phone. These checks happen before the preview reaches the approval chat.

## Review once, publish deliberately

The final preview contains the actual media and every target's copy. Approval applies to those exact files and words. If either changes, the draft needs another review. This is a practical way to avoid approving one version and accidentally publishing another.

After publication, I save the returned identifiers and check the resulting links. A failed platform can resume from a saved checkpoint, while a completed platform stays untouched. Corrections go into the next post. The checklist ends with a short report that makes the outcome clear: what succeeded, what still needs attention, and which local article files are ready to commit.
